procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Patna High Court dated December 17, 1963, which allowed the revision petition, set aside the order of the Munsif, and directed the executing court to deliver possession of the land to the respondent.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent filed a revision petition under sec. 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the Munsif's order dismissing the respondent's application under 0.21 r. 97 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court allowed the revision petition, set aside the Munsif's order, and directed the executing court to deliver possession of the land to the respondent.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave from the judgment and order of the Patna High Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal with costs.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal is dismissed with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether a real owner is bound by a decision in proceedings brought by or against his benamidar, even when the real owner was not formally a party to those proceedings.

law.law_text: The Court affirmed the well-settled legal principle that in litigation with a third party, a benamidar represents the real owner.

The benamidar is considered a mere trustee for the real owner, and therefore, a decision in a proceeding brought by or against the benamidar is fully binding on the real owner under the rules of res judicata.
This rule applies even if the real owner is not formally joined as a party to the proceedings.
An exception to this rule exists if it can be shown that the benamidar could not, or did not, in fact, represent the interests of the real owner in that proceeding.

application.application_text: The Court examined the facts and found that the benamidar (Lakhan Lal) and his heirs had fully represented the appellant (the real owner) in the prior proceedings.

It was noted that the appellant had actively conducted the proceedings himself as the attorney for the benamidar, and after the benamidar's death, his heirs continued to press all the contentions that could be advanced on the appellant's behalf.
The Court determined that the non-joinder of the appellant as a formal party did not cause him any prejudice, as his interests were vigorously defended.
Since the benamidar had effectively represented the real owner's interests, the exception to the general rule did not apply.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the real owner was bound by the decree passed in the previous proceedings against his benamidar (and the benamidar's heirs) because the benamidar had fully and effectively represented the real owner's interests throughout the litigation.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Munsif's observation that the appellant would not be bound by the decree, made while dismissing the application to be added as a party, operates as res judicata.

facts: When the Munsif dismissed the appellant's application to be added as a party to the original suit, the Munsif observed that the appellant would not be bound by the decree.
Later, in execution proceedings, the Munsif relied on this earlier observation to dismiss the respondent's application against the appellant.
law: For a finding or observation to operate as res judicata, the question it addresses must have been an actual issue in the proceeding where the finding was made.
application: The Supreme Court found that the question of whether the appellant would be bound by the final decree was not an issue before the Munsif when he was deciding the procedural application to add a party.
The Munsif's role at that stage was simply to decide whether to add the appellant as a defendant, not to determine the ultimate effect of the decree on him.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that since the matter was not in issue, the Munsif's observation was merely an "expression of opinion" and could not operate as res judicata to prevent the courts from later deciding that the appellant was, in fact, bound by the decree.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court had the power under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside the Munsif's order in the execution proceedings.

facts: The appellant argued that the High Court lacked the power under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside the Munsif's order.
This specific legal point was not raised by the appellant in the High Court; it was a new contention brought before the Supreme Court.
The respondent had already been deprived of the property for over 16 years since the original award was made.
application: The Supreme Court refused to allow the appellant to raise this new contention for the first time.
The Court reasoned that permitting this new argument would result in a "grave miscarriage of justice."

It noted that if the High Court had dismissed the case on this jurisdictional ground, the respondent would have pursued a different legal remedy (a suit under O.21 r. 23 C.P.C.) to which the appellant would have had no defense.
Given the long delay and the injustice to the respondent, the Court decided that the "ends of justice" required that the appellant not be permitted to raise this new point.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument without deciding on its legal merits. It concluded that it would be unjust to allow the appellant to raise this new jurisdictional issue so late in the proceedings, and therefore it was not necessary to determine whether the High Court actually had the power under Section 115.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a real owner is bound by a decision in proceedings brought by or against his benamidar, even when the real owner was not formally a party to those proceedings.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that as the real owner, he was not bound by the decree passed against his benamidar, especially since his application to be added as a party to the original proceedings had been rejected.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the appellant, as the real owner, is bound by the decree. The benamidar's heirs contested the suit on behalf of the real owner, and all contentions that could have been advanced by the appellant were put forward and vigorously pressed, so he suffered no prejudice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Munsif's observation that the appellant would not be bound by the decree, made while dismissing the application to be added as a party, operates as res judicata.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's position was that the Munsif's observation during the execution proceedings—that the appellant was not bound by the decree because his earlier application to be joined was rejected—should be treated as final and operate as res judicata.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the Munsif's observation could not operate as res judicata because the question of whether the appellant would be bound by the decree was not formally in issue when the Munsif was deciding the application to add him as a party.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court had the power under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside the Munsif's order in the execution proceedings.
appellant_arguments: The appellant submitted that the High Court had no power under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside the Munsif's order.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the appellant should not be allowed to raise this contention for the first time in the Supreme Court. Allowing it would lead to a grave miscarriage of justice, as the respondent had been deprived of the property for over 16 years, and had the High Court dismissed the petition on this ground, the respondent would have immediately filed a suit to establish his right.

cases.case_name: Gur Narayan v. Sheo Lal Singh
cases.principle: To establish that a benamidar represents the real owner in a suit, and consequently, a decree against the benamidar is binding on the real owner.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In litigation with a third party, a benamidar sufficiently represents the real owner. A decision in a proceeding by or against the benamidar is fully binding on the real owner under the rules of res judicata, regardless of whether the real owner was made a party to the action.
obiter: In a contest between an alleged benamidar and an alleged real owner, other considerations arise.
The ends of justice require that a party ought not to be permitted to raise a new contention at a late stage of litigation if it would lead to a grave miscarriage of justice.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant, as the real owner, is bound by the decree passed in the earlier suit against his benamidar. The decree can be executed against him under O. 21 r. 35 C.P.C., and he is therefore bound to vacate the property.
legal_tests_applied: In a proceeding by or against the benamidar, the person beneficially entitled is fully affected by the rules of res judicata. It is open to the latter to apply to be joined in the action; but whether he is made a party or not, a proceeding by or against his representatives in its ultimate result is fully binding on him.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant is bound by the decree against his benamidar because the benamidar represents the real owner. The court found that the non-joinder of the appellant as a party did not cause him any prejudice, as all the contentions which could be advanced on his behalf were put forward by the benamidar's heirs and vigorously pressed.

The Munsif's observation that the appellant would not be bound by the decree could not operate as res judicata because the question of whether he would be bound was not formally in issue before the Munsif when the observation was made.

The appellant was not permitted to raise the contention that the High Court lacked power under s. 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure because the point was not taken in the High Court, and allowing it to be raised for the first time would cause a grave miscarriage of justice.
why_respondent_won: The decree against the benamidar was fully binding on the appellant as the real owner, in line with the established legal principle that a benamidar represents the real owner in legal proceedings.
The Munsif's earlier observation did not have the force of res judicata because it was an expression of opinion on a question that was not formally in issue in that proceeding.

The court refused to entertain the appellant's new argument regarding the High Court's jurisdiction on grounds of fairness, noting that the respondent had been deprived of the property for over 16 years and would have filed a separate suit had the jurisdictional issue been raised earlier.
policy_considerations: The ends of justice require that the appellant ought not to be permitted to raise this new contention now.

If the court allows the appellant to raise the contention regarding the High Court's jurisdiction for the first time, there will be a grave miscarriage of justice, as the respondent has been deprived of the property for over 16 years.
